Something is passing through you right now.
Roughly a hundred trillion tiny particles, every single second.
To see where most of the ones around us come from, we have to leave this room, leave Earth, and dive straight into the Sun.
Deep in its core, atomic nuclei fuse together.
As the Sun makes the energy that keeps Earth alive, it also releases streams of these ghostlike messengers.
They race outward at almost the speed of light.
And some can even change from one kind of neutrino into another as they travel.
For most of these particles, even an entire planet is surprisingly easy to pass through.
Including the ground beneath your feet.
Not because atoms are just empty holes.
Neutrinos have no electric charge, and they interact with ordinary matter incredibly rarely.
Imagine an entire city where almost every door is invisible to you.
So how do scientists study something that almost never touches anything?
They build a detector so enormous that, eventually, one of those incredibly rare interactions becomes visible.
Deep in Antarctic ice, thousands of sensors wait in a cubic kilometer of crystal-clear darkness.
When a sufficiently energetic neutrino interacts, the charged particles it creates can produce a sudden flash of blue light.
Scientists don't see the neutrino directly.
They see the light and reconstruct what happened.
Some of these messengers have travelled from violent events far beyond our solar system.
So the universe is not just something you look at.
Most of it will leave no trace.
But once in a while, it tells us a story.
